blocks.text: Biologists group living things so that their evolutionary relationships are easier to see. In 1969 the American ecologist Robert Whittaker placed all organisms in five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia. Kingdom Monera held the prokaryotes, cells without a nucleus. The other four kingdoms held eukaryotes.

In 1990 the American microbiologist Carl Woese argued that prokaryotes are not one group. He separated them into Archaea and Bacteria and, on that basis, arranged all life into three domains: domain Archaea, domain Bacteria and domain Eukarya. Archaea and Bacteria are both prokaryotic, but they differ in several features.

blocks.title: Phylogeny
blocks.text: The evolutionary relationship among organisms is called phylogeny. A diagram that shows phylogeny is a phylogenetic tree, also called an evolutionary tree.

blocks.alt: Evolutionary tree of the three domains. A single trunk from the Common Ancestor splits in two: one branch leads to Domain Bacteria, drawn as a green cluster of many radiating lineages; the other divides again into Domain Archaea, a yellow cluster of lineages, and Domain Eukarya, a blue cluster of lineages.
blocks.caption: Figure 1.1: Evolutionary tree of the three domains (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 1.1).

blocks.text: In the five-kingdom system this domain sat inside kingdom Monera. The name comes from the Greek archaios, meaning ancient. Archaea are prokaryotes that diverged from bacteria in very ancient times. An individual archaean is 0.1 micrometre to more than 15 micrometres across. Some form aggregates or filaments up to 200 micrometres long. Their shapes include spherical, rod-shaped, spiral, lobed and rectangular cells. They reproduce asexually by binary or multiple fission, fragmentation or budding. Mitosis and meiosis do not occur in archaea. Archaea were at first classified as a group of bacteria and were called archaebacteria.

Cell membrane. The membrane lipids of archaea have an ether linkage between glycerol and the fatty acid chains, and the chains are branched. That is why their membranes resist extreme conditions. Bacteria and Eukarya instead have fatty acids attached to glycerol by ester linkages, and their chains are unbranched.

Cell wall composition. The cell walls of archaea lack cellulose and peptidoglycan. Instead they contain distinct polysaccharides and proteins; some archaea have pseudopeptidoglycan. Bacterial cell walls contain peptidoglycan, a polymer of sugars and amino acids that provides structural support. In Eukarya a cell wall, when present, is made of cellulose in plants or chitin in fungi.
Genetic differences. Archaea share several genetic sequences and regulatory features with eukaryotes, which highlights their closer evolutionary relationship to Eukarya.

Metabolism. Archaea have unique metabolic processes such as methanogenesis, the production of methane, which is found in neither bacteria nor Eukarya. Bacteria show metabolic pathways that include photosynthesis, nitrogen fixation and fermentation. In Eukarya the metabolic processes are often more complex and include cellular respiration, photosynthesis in plants and algae, and various forms of fermentation.

items: Methanogens produce methane as a metabolic by-product.
Halobacteria live in extremely saline (salty) environments.
Thermococci are found in hot environments.
Thaumarchaeota are involved in the nitrogen cycle.

blocks.title: Significance of Archaea
blocks.text: Archaeans that live in high acidity and alkalinity are a source of enzymes that work under harsh conditions. The enzymes of DNA replication extracted from such archaeans work best at high temperatures and allow rapid cloning of DNA in the laboratory. Methanogen archaeans are a vital part of sewage treatment: they carry out anaerobic digestion and produce biogas. Acidophilic archaea are used to extract metals such as gold, cobalt and copper from ores in mineral processing. In humans, intestinal gas is largely the result of the metabolism of methanogens.
In the five-kingdom system this domain was also placed in kingdom Monera. These are the true bacteria. They have several distinct characteristics that separate them from Archaea and Eukarya.

items: Cell structure: like archaea, bacteria have prokaryotic cells, with no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.
Cell wall composition: the wall is made of peptidoglycan, a unique polymer that gives structural support and shape.
Genetic material: a single circular chromosome of DNA lies in the nucleoid region.
Plasmids: most bacteria carry small circular DNA molecules that can be transferred between bacteria, aiding genetic diversity and adaptation.
Reproduction: mainly asexual, by binary fission, in which one cell divides into two identical daughter cells.
Nutritional modes: autotrophs (self-feeding, for example photosynthetic bacteria) and heterotrophs (feeding on organic matter, for example decomposers).
Morphology: cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), spirilla (spiral-shaped) and vibrios (comma-shaped).
Arrangement: singly, in pairs (diplococci), in chains (streptococci), in clusters (staphylococci) or in other species-specific arrangements.
Flagella: many bacteria have one or more whip-like flagella for movement.
Pili and fimbriae: hair-like structures in some bacteria that help attachment to surfaces and the exchange of genetic material.
Respiration: bacteria can be obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes, microaerophiles or aerotolerant anaerobes. Some perform fermentation to get energy without oxygen.
Extremophiles: some thrive at high temperature (thermophiles), high salinity (halophiles) or low pH (acidophiles).
Pathogenicity: some cause disease in humans, animals and plants by producing toxins or other virulence factors.
Symbiosis: many live with other organisms in mutualism (both benefit) or commensalism (one benefits, the other is not harmed).

blocks.text: The domain Bacteria is divided into numerous groups, for example:

items: Proteobacteria, for example Escherichia coli, Rhizobium and Helicobacter pylori.
Firmicutes, for example Bacillus subtilis, Lactobacillus and Clostridium botulinum.
Actinobacteria, for example Streptomyces and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Cyanobacteria, for example Anabaena and Spirulina.
Spirochaetes, for example Treponema pallidum.
Acidobacteria, for example Acidobacterium.
Aquificae, for example Aquifex pyrophilus.

blocks.text: Domain Eukarya includes all organisms with eukaryotic cells, which are fundamentally different from the prokaryotic cells of Bacteria and Archaea. These are the general characteristics that justify treating Eukarya as a separate domain.

items: Cell structure: a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane, and membrane-bounded organelles such as mitochondria, chloroplasts (in plants and algae), endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes. A cytoskeleton of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments gives structural support, enables cell movement and moves materials inside the cell.
Genetic material: DNA is organised into multiple linear chromosomes inside the nucleus, associated with histone proteins that help organise and regulate it.

Reproduction: most eukaryotes reproduce sexually, through meiosis and fertilisation, which creates genetic diversity. Some also reproduce asexually by mitosis, producing genetically identical offspring.
Complex cellular organisation: in multicellular eukaryotes, cells differentiate into specialised types that form tissues and organs with specific functions.

Evolutionary relationships: eukaryotes are believed to have originated through endosymbiosis, in which certain prokaryotic cells (which became mitochondria and chloroplasts) were engulfed by a host cell, leading to a symbiotic relationship.
